query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding minor amounts of yttrium and hafnium to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature and long‐term mechanical stability (including creep resistance) as well as its corrosion resistance without sacrificing its strength–ductility balance, by promoting interfacial segregation that improves the adhesion of the protective oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a fine, uniform lamellar microstructure (fcc/B2) that delivers good strength and plasticity yet shows limitations in stability under cyclic extreme temperatures, long-term load (creep), and corrosive environments.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by co‐doping it with small, controlled amounts of reactive elements—specifically yttrium (Y) and hafnium (Hf)—integrated during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated service conditions such as cyclic thermal fluctuations (mimicking aircraft/spacecraft fastener environments), sustained room‐temperature mechanical loading to assess creep behavior, and exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing sulfuric acid or molten salt mixtures at elevated temperatures).
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with the additional segregation of yttrium and hafnium at phase and grain boundaries and on surfaces, which promotes the formation of a more adherent and stable protective oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The reactive elements (Y and Hf) are expected to segregate to critical interfaces, where they lower local boundary energy and enhance oxide scale adhesion. This stabilizes the microstructure during thermal cycling, retards diffusional creep, and decreases corrosion attack (by reducing pitting and scale spallation), all while maintaining the favorable balance of strength and ductility inherent to the original lamellar structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y/Hf co-doped alloy will exhibit slower room-temperature creep, improved resistance to microstructural coarsening under extreme temperature fluctuations, and lower spallation/pitting in corrosive tests—with minimal impact on its high strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy produced by conventional casting, which—despite its good mechanical performance—is limited by age-related microstructural instability, susceptibility to creep, and less-than-optimal corrosion resistance under extreme operational conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefits of Y/Hf doping are expected only within a narrow compositional window; excessive additions or alterations that disrupt the inherited lamellar microstructure may negate the advantages. The improvement is also specific to the intended environmental conditions and may not translate to drastically different loading or corrosive media.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum concentrations of Y and Hf, the quantitative changes in creep rate and corrosion metrics, and any subtle impacts on ductility under complex loading remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and a second set modified with controlled minor additions of Y and Hf. Subject both sets to (a) cyclic thermal fluctuation tests mimicking aerospace temperature profiles, (b) long-term room-temperature creep testing under sustained load, and (c) hot corrosion tests in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid environment or molten salt at elevated temperature. Analyze changes in microstructure and mechanical performance before and after exposure.
measurements: Creep rate (strain vs. time under constant load) at room temperature
Degree of oxide scale spallation and pitting density via SEM and image analysis
Tensile strength and ductility (yield and ultimate stress, elongation) pre- and post-exposure
Microstructural observations (grain size, phase stability) using TEM/SEM/XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf co-doped samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in creep resistance, thermal stability (i.e., less grain coarsening or phase instability), and corrosion performance (reduced spallation/pitting) compared with the baseline alloy—without a marked loss in strength or ductility—the hypothesis should be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1.
